documentation.range: The Greater Glider occurs in the eucalypt forests of eastern Australia, mainly along the east coast and near-coastal ranges, from sea level to approximately 1,200 m asl. It has a broad distribution from the Windsor Tableland in Queensland in the north, to the coast of Victoria in the south. There is a gap in distribution in the region of the Burdekin River, separating a small north-eastern portion of the range extending from Townsville north to the Windsor Tableland, from a much larger southern portion that extends southward from around Rockhampton. These two disjunct areas of distribution are considered as distinct subspecies, P. volans minor in the north and P. v. volans in the south. The westernmost occurrence is in the Wombat State Forest in central Victoria.
documentation.population:
There is no reliable estimate of population size. Lunney et al. (2008) considered that the species had a ‘presumed large population’ and was ‘locally common’. In New South Wales, Kavanagh (2004) considered it ‘widespread and common … particularly in north-eastern New South Wales’. Density estimates in Victoria range from 0.6 to 2.8 individuals/ha (Henry 1984, van der Ree et al. 2004), and across its broader range from 0.01 to 5 individuals/ha (Kavanagh 1984, Kehl and Borsboom 1984, Maloney 2007). In a locally abundant population in the northern part of the species range, Comport et al. (1996) estimated a density of 2.6-5.8 animals/ha. Population estimates are available for some sites: Goldingay et al. (2022) estimated that there were more than 2,400 mature Greater Gliders in a 157 km² national park in northern New South Wales. Cripps et al. (2021) estimated that there were 24,575 greater gliders (of all ages) in the 259 km² Strathbogie Ranges in Victoria. These estimates of density together with the wide distribution of the species demonstrate that the total population is well over 100,000.

Populations that have been monitored over the last 10 years or more show consistent evidence of decline, in some cases to local extinction. For example, declines in occupancy and detection rate in standardised surveys have been recorded for over more than two decades of monitoring in the Victorian Central Highlands (Lumsden et al. 2013, Lindenmayer 2020, Lindenmayer et al. 2024). There have been losses of subpopulations in NSW within the Jervis Bay and Blue Mountains areas (Lindenmayer et al. 2011, Smith and Smith 2018). In addition, the species was badly affected by the 2019–2020 bushfires, which severely affected much of its forest habitat in southeastern Australia. Post-fire surveys have indicated that in areas of high fire severity there is zero to very low occupancy (Smith and Smith 2022). A systematic analysis using mapping of fire severity classes over the species' distribution linked to expert elicitation to estimate effects on abundance concluded that there was an overall population decline of >20% one year after the fires, which is expected to increase to >30% within three generations after the fires (Legge et al. 2022).
documentation.habitats:
The Greater Glider is an arboreal marsupial of eastern Australian eucalypt forests and woodlands. Typically, it is most abundant in taller, montane, moist eucalypt forests, that have relatively old trees and abundant hollows (Andrews et al. 1994; Smith et al. 1994a,b; Kavanagh 2000; Eyre 2004; van der Ree et al. 2004; Vanderduys et al. 2012). The species' distribution may be patchy even in suitable habitat (Kavanagh 2000). The Greater Glider favours forests with a diversity of eucalypt species, due to seasonal variation in preference for food tree species (Kavanagh 1984).

The species is primarily folivorous, with a diet mostly comprising eucalypt leaves, and occasionally flowers and buds (Kehl and Borsboom 1984, Kavanagh and Lambert 1990, van der Ree et al. 2004). It feeds on a limited number of eucalypt species, and preferences for tree species vary regionally. Forests with high diversity of tree species are most valuable, because diversity compensates for seasonal differences in foliage production and nutrient composition among species. Approximately 85% of the Greater Glider’s water requirements are provided by consumed leaves (Foley et al. 1990). Free water is presumably obtained from dew condensation on leaf surfaces (Rübsamen et al. 1984).

During the day the Greater Glider shelters in tree hollows, requiring large hollows in large, old trees (Henry 1984, Kehl and Borsboom 1984, Lindenmayer et al. 1991, Smith et al. 2007, Goldingay 2012). In the Grafton/Casino, Urbenville and Urunga/Coffs Harbour Forestry Management Areas (FMAs) in northern New South Wales, the abundance of Greater Gliders on survey sites was significantly greater on sites with a higher abundance of tree hollows (Andrews et al. 1994, Smith et al. 1994a,b). In the Grafton/Casino FMA, the Greater Glider was absent from surveyed sites with fewer than six tree hollows per hectare (Smith et al. 1994a). In southern Queensland, Greater Gliders need at least 2-4 live den trees for every 2 ha of suitable forest habitat (Eyre 2002). Comport et al. (1996) found that individuals used 4-6 different dens over the course of a month.

Home ranges are typically relatively small (1–4 ha: Henry 1984, Kehl and Borsboom 1984, Comport et al. 1996, Gibbons and Lindenmayer 2002, Pope et al. 2005), but are larger in forests of lower productivity and woodlands that are more open (to 16 ha: Eyre 2004, Smith et al. 2007, McGregor et al. 2023), and larger for males than for females (Kavanagh and Wheeler 2004, Pope et al. 2005). Home ranges of males are mostly non-overlapping (Henry 1984, Kavanagh and Wheeler 2004, Pope et al. 2005).

The greater glider is highly sensitive to forest clearance (Tyndale-Biscoe and Smith 1969a), and to intensive logging (Kavanagh and Bamkin 1995, Kavanagh and Webb 1998, Kavanagh and Wheeler 2004, Kavanagh et al. 1995), although responses vary according to landscape context and the extent of tree removal and retention (Kavanagh 2000, Taylor et al. 2007). The species is also sensitive to wildfire (Lunney 1987, Andrews et al. 1994, Lindenmayer et al. 2011, Smith and Smith 2022, Green et al. 2024), and local populations are slow to recover following major disturbance (Kavanagh 2004) because of low rates of increase and low immigration rates due to limited dispersal capacity. In Urbenville FMA of northern New South Wales, the abundance of Greater Gliders on survey sites was significantly greater in forests that were infrequently burnt (Andrews et al. 1994).

Greater Gilders are sensitive to effects of habitat fragmentation (Eyre 2006, McCarthy and Lindenmayer 1999ab, Lindenmayer et al. 2000, Taylor and Goldingay 2009), because they have relatively low persistence in small forest fragments and disperse poorly across vegetation that is not native forest. Modelling suggests that they need native forest patches of at least 160 km² to maintain viable populations (Eyre 2002).

Females give birth to a single young, from March to June (Tyndale-Biscoe and Smith 1969b, McKay 2008). Sexual maturity is reached in the second year (Tyndale-Biscoe and Smith 1969b). Longevity has been estimated at 15 years (Harris and Maloney 2010), so generation length is ca 7 years (TSSC 2023a). The relatively low reproductive rate (Henry 1984) may render small, isolated populations in small remnants prone to extinction (van der Ree 2004, Pope et al. 2005).
documentation.threats:
The most significant threats are increased intensity and frequency of bushfires (linked to climate change); increased temperature and changed rainfall patterns due to climate change; inappropriate prescribed burning; habitat clearing and fragmentation; and timber harvesting.

Increased intensity and frequency of bushfires
Large losses or declines, including disappearance of local populations, have been documented following high-severity fires (McLean et al. 2018, Smith and Smith 2022, Green et al. 2024). These effects may be the result of direct mortality from lethal heating or suffocation, or loss of key habitat features and resources. Following the 2009 Victorian bushfires, 79% of large living trees with cavities died in the affected Eucalyptus regnans (Mountain Ash) forests; recruitment of new cavities takes many years (Lindenmayer et al. 2012). Populations have disappeared after major fires. The effects of fire can be compounded by habitat fragmentation, because the species does not readily disperse over gaps in forest habitat and so is slow to recolonise areas recovering from fire. No individuals were recorded for 19 years after a fire in an isolated area of habitat in Royal National Park near Sydney (Andrews et al. 2014). Recurring fires can therefore cause progressive regional decline in the proportion of forest habitat occupied. Indicators of forest fire danger in southeastern Australia point to an increase in the threat of severe fire in the near future, driven mainly by climate change (Boer et al. 2020). More than 23% of the temperate forests of southeastern Australia were burnt in the 2019-2020 fire season. The conditions that cause these extreme fires are intensifying.

Increased temperatures and changed rainfall patterns
Mean temperatures across the distribution of Greater Glider have risen by 1.4 degrees over the past century, and heat waves have become longer and more frequent (BOM and CSIRO 2020). In the southern part of the range, winter rainfall has declined by 12% since the 1990s, but summer rainfall remains unchanged. These trends are projected to continue under moderate and high emissions scenarios (CSIRO and BOM 2021). 

A unique physiology and strict eucalypt diet make the Greater Glider vulnerable to high temperatures and low water availability (Rübsamen et al. 1984). Prolonged exposure to temperatures over 40°C is likely to lead to high mortality (Rübsamen et al. 1984). Moore et al. (2004) suggested that the preference of Greater Gliders for higher elevations is because they are sensitive to heat and must expend energy and water to cool themselves at ambient temperatures over 20°C. Increased night-time temperatures have been implicated in the decline of abundance in Victorian subpopulations (Wagner et al. 2020). At lower altitude (<500 m) sites surveyed in the Blue Mountains, increasing mean annual temperatures were considered to be the cause of declines of Greater Gliders (Smith and Smith 2018, 2020). A marked reduction in detection rates was reported for greater gliders in forests in northern New South Wales during periods of drought (Goldingay et al. 2022).

Water stress limits growth in forest eucalypts (Matusick et al. 2013) and reduces availability of browse. Combined with high temperature this may cause heat stress, drought stress and mortality (Vic SAC 2015). Extended droughts in a warmer climate are likely to reduce the quality of available foliage (e.g. young foliage is more palatable than older foliage; McKeirnan et al. 2014) for Greater Gliders, and could therefore reduce reproduction rates (DeGabriel et al. 2009, Kearney et al. 2010). Above temperatures of 35℃, Greater Gliders need to dissipate >100% of metabolic heat production by evaporative means (Rübasamen 1984). At the same time, they reduce their food intake, leading to rapid expenditure of their energy and water stores (Beale et al. 2018, Youngentob et al. 2021). This can lead to death of both young and adult gliders, or reduced growth in milk-fed young (Youngentob et al. 2021). Climate projections and biophysical modelling of the Greater Glider in the northern portion of its range (that is, for the subspecies P. volans minor) predict a severe range contraction and increase in fragmentation of the remaining range under a 3°C temperature increase (Kearney et al. 2010).

Inappropriate prescribed burning practices
In Victoria, loss of hollow-bearing trees due to mechanical site-preparation works associated with prescribed burning may reduce suitable habitat for the Greater Glider. This impact occurs primarily in foothill forests close to settled areas. Trees that are assessed as potentially hazardous (if they were to catch fire) are routinely removed from the perimeter of planned burns on public land in Victoria. They are also removed from bushfire control lines during and after bushfire suppression activities (DELWP n.d). Although not all hazardous trees are hollow-bearing, many are.

Too intense or frequent planned burning may contribute to population losses or declines in the southern part of the Greater Glider’s range. Bluff (2016) reported that hollow-bearing trees affected by fire during planned burns were 28 times more likely to collapse than those that were not burnt. Parnaby et al. (2010) found that following low intensity prescription burns in the Pilliga forests (NSW), mean collapse rates for burnt hollow-bearing trees were 14-26%. This was consistent with the collapse rate of 25.6% found by Bluff (2016). A survey following a planned burn at Tallarook Range (NSW) in 2021 found that a large number of potential Greater Glider habitat trees were burnt, with “many destroyed” (N. Stimson 2021, pers. comm. 26 June, cited in TSSC 2022a).

After fires, trees with large hollows are often felled for safety reasons (along roads, fire trails and walking trails) within Greater Glider habitat (DECCW 2011). Andrew (2001) reported that 120 hollow-bearing trees were felled after the 1994 bushfires in Royal National Park by NPWS due to concerns over public safety.

Habitat clearing and fragmentation
The Greater Glider is absent from cleared areas and has little dispersal ability to move through cleared areas between fragments (Tyndale-Biscoe and Smith 1969b; McCarthy and Lindenmayer 1999a,b; Lindenmayer et al. 2000; Eyre 2006; Taylor and Goldingay 2009). Population viability in small remnants is low due to the species’ low reproductive output and susceptibility to disturbance and edge effects. Extensive land clearing for development and agriculture has led to fragmentation of habitat in some areas, e.g. the Tumut area of NSW (Pope et al. 2005) where small subpopulations exist in a pine matrix. About 30 years after clearing in the Tumut area, Lindenmayer et al. (1999) found that the occupancy rate of Greater Gliders in remnant patches was 21% compared to 38% in the surrounding native forest, indicating limited recolonisation. The probability of occurrence was significantly greater in large remnants. Genetic analysis in the Tumut population by Taylor et al. (2007) indicated that some immigration into patches was occurring, but there were lower levels of immigration and genetic mixing in patches further (>1 km) from continuous forest.

Timber harvesting
The sensitivity of Greater Gliders to timber harvesting has been well documented. Although much habitat across the species’ range is found in conservation reserves (Smith and Smith 2018, Wagner et al. 2020), where timber harvesting is excluded and the removal of hollow-bearing trees is subject to constraints, much prime habitat coincides with areas suitable for timber harvesting (Braithwaite 1984). There is a progressive decline in numbers of hollow-bearing trees in some production forests, as harvesting rotations become shorter and dead stags collapse, and hollow-bearing trees are not replaced due to lack of recruitment (Ross 1999; Ball et al. 1999; Lindenmayer et al. 2011, 2012).

The degree of impact depends on forest type and timber harvesting intensity, with larger declines in more heavily logged sites (Tyndale-Biscoe and Smith 1969b, Lunney 1987, Kavanagh et al. 1995, Kavanagh and Webb 1998, Kavanagh 2000, McLean et al. 2018). In the Central Highlands of Victoria, where clear-felling is undertaken, Lindenmayer et al. (2017b) found that the rate of loss of hollow-bearing trees greatly exceeded the rate of recruitment. The area of clear-felled forest adjacent to wildlife corridors was also found to increase the chance of collapse of hollow-bearing trees, possibly due to the greater exposure of stems to elevated wind speeds at corridor edges. However, models investigating the impacts of forest disturbance on the Greater Glider in the same area found that timber harvesting in the surrounding landscape was not a significant influence on the probability of occurrence of the species (Lindenmayer et al. 2020).

Recovery of subpopulations following timber harvesting is slow. Subpopulations in south-east New South Wales had not recovered 8 years after timber harvesting in sites retaining 62%, 52% and 21% of the original tree basal area (Kavanagh and Webb 1998). In the regrowth Mountain Ash forests (Central Highlands) of Vic, Greater Gliders (southern and central) were absent post-timber harvesting until the forests were >38 years old (Macfarlane 1988).

Concerns about the conservation of greater gliders in production forests has been a high-profile issue and timber harvesting has been subject to many legal challenges (Wardell-Johnson and Robinson 2022). Partly as a consequence, the Victorian government ceased harvesting of native forests in 2024.
documentation.measures:
The Greater Glider occurs in many conservation reserves across its extensive range. In production forests, some logging prescriptions have been imposed to reduce impacts upon this species. The Victorian government ceased logging in native forests in 2024.

The species is listed as Endangered (as ‘greater glider (southern and central) Petauroides volans’) and Vulnerable (as ‘greater glider (northern) P. minor’) under Australian law, with conservation advices to guide management (Threatened Species Scientific Committee 2022a,b). However, such management and legal protection has been ineffective at halting decline (Ashman et al. 2021).
documentation.rationale:
The Greater Glider is endemic to Australia. The species is assessed as Endangered (EN A2ab+4abc), based on evidence of recent and likely future rates of population decline and decline in habitat quality. The population of the Greater Glider is declining because of habitat loss, fragmentation, extensive fire, climate change, and some forestry practices. The species is particularly susceptible because of slow life history characteristics, specialist requirements for large tree hollows (and hence mature forests), and relatively specialised dietary requirements. Across its broad range, the population size and rate of decline is incompletely known, but several large-scale monitoring programs have demonstrated substantial declines. A large-scale (ca 160 monitoring sites across the Central Highlands, Victoria), long-term (1997 to 2024) monitoring program reported declines of about 80% in the probability of occurrence of this species (Lindenmayer et al. 2021, 2024). A substantial monitoring program in a conservation reserve in coastal New South Wales reported a complete loss of the monitored subpopulation over the period 2002 to 2010 (Lindenmayer et al. 2011). Smith and Smith (2020) reported major declines in lower altitude forests of the Blue Mountains, with sampling in 2015–2016 failing to record the species in seven of 20 sites at which it was known in the 1980s. An ongoing monitoring program (from 2014) in forests of northern New South Wales reported a 60–70% decline in probability of detection, with decline coinciding with low rainfall years (Goldingay et al. 2022). At woodland sites in central Queensland first sampled in 1973–1976 and re-sampled in 2001–2002, abundance declined by 89% (Woinarski et al. 2006). 

Large areas of the habitat of the Greater Glider were affected by the catastrophic bushfires of the summer of 2019/2020. A systematic analysis using mapping of fire severity classes over the species' distribution linked to expert elicitation to estimate effects on abundance concluded that there was an overall population decline of >20% one year after the fires, which is expected to increase to >30% within three generations after the fires (Legge et al. 2022). Subsequent sampling indicates that these fires did indeed cause major reductions in population size (Smith and Smith 2022, Green et al. 2024).

The Commonwealth of Australia Threatened Species Scientific Committee (TSSC 2022a), taking into account both the effects of the 2019/20 bushfires and other evidence on declines not related to those events, estimated that the overall rate of decline exceeds 50% over three generations (21 years). Current declines are likely to continue, as the causes of decline are still operating. This estimate of decline rate applies to the subspecies P. v. volans. There is no monitoring of populations of the northern subspecies P. volans minor. However, the northern subspecies is subject to many of the same threats as P. v. volans, and is also likely to be in decline. The subspecies P. v. volans represents the great majority of the distribution of P. volans (approx. 95%, Woinarski et al. 2014). It is therefore unlikely that a lower decline rate of P. v. minor could offset the declines recorded by monitoring of P. v. volans and justify an assessment of Vulnerable (VU) rather than EN (the subspecies P. v. minor is treated as a full species by the Australian Commonwealth and is listed as VU under Commonwealth legislation (TSSC 2022b), on the basis that modelling of the impacts of climate change indicated that populations might decline by approximately 30% over the next three generations (Kearney et al. 2010), together with its small area of occupancy and number of locations).
documentation.taxonomic_notes: The taxonomic treatment of Petauroides volans is contested and not fully resolved. A single species has long been accepted. However, Jackson (2015) and Jackson and Groves (2015) recognised three species: Petauroides volans, P. minor and P. armillatus, based on limited published evidence. A subsequent genetic study provided some support to this treatment (McGregor et al. 2020), and the three species are currently listed in the American Society of Mammalogists Mammal Diversity Database (version 1.13). In its most recent conservation assessment, the Australian government recognised two species: P. volans (including P. armillatus) and P. minor (Threatened Species Scientific Committee 2022a,b). However, that split is not recognised in a recent taxonomic review of Australasian marsupials (Baker et al. 2023), by the Australasian Mammal Taxonomy Consortium (as at August 2024) and, following this, by Jackson (2023). The previous Red List account was for the single species, P. volans; until the taxonomy is fully resolved, and the IUCN SSC Australasian Marsupial and Monotreme Specialist Group continues to follow this treatment.
